articles.title: Pakistan’s reforms deficit
articles.content: PAKISTAN has never suffered from a shortage of civil service reform proposals. It has suffered from a shortage of reforms that survive implementation. Since independence, successive governments, commissions and committees have attempted to restructure the administrative machinery inherited from the colonial state. Yet familiar complaints persist: excessive generalism, weak accountability, politicisation, distorted incentives, slow decision-making and a bureaucracy often better equipped to process files than solve complex problems. The latest reform package is significant not because Pakistan has rediscovered civil service reform, but because it attempts to address several structural weaknesses simultaneously. It proposes 11 specialised professional cadres, competency-based recruitment, performance-linked remuneration, restructuring of training and human-resource management, and a National Executive Service (NES) under which BS-20 and above positions could be opened to serving officials, academics and private-sector professionals. Pakistan inherited the powerful, generalist Civil Service of Pakistan from the colonial administrative tradition. The most dramatic restructuring came under Zulfikar Ali Bhutto in 1973, when the CSP structure was abolished and occupational groups reorganised. But restructuring did not democratise opportunity within government. The devolution reforms introduced under Gen Pervez Musharraf in 2001 represented another major intervention, transferring substantial authority towards elected local governments and altering traditional district administration. But institutional discontinuity and subsequent political changes prevented the system from developing into a durable architecture of local governance. Reform is often treated as an event rather than a sustained process. This history reveals Pakistan’s recurring problem: reform is often treated as an event rather than a sustained process. The strongest feature of the present package is its recognition that a modern state cannot be managed through transferable generalists. Professional cadres in fields including IT and telecom, energy, climate, engineering, health, education, law, agriculture and science address a genuine administrative weakness. Opening senior positions to competition could be still more consequential. It could bring specialists into government who would otherwise never enter conventional public service and allow capable career officers to compete beyond rigid cadre boundaries. But lateral entry carries an equally obvious risk: without credible safeguards, it can become lateral patronage. International experience offers principles rather than readymade templates. Pakistan should borrow principles, not blindly transplant institutions. Performance-linked remuneration illustrates the challenge. Annual performance agreements for ministries, flowing down to individual officers, could improve accountability. But who determines whether a secretary has performed well? If targets are vague or assessments depend excessively upon political superiors, financial incentives could reward proximity to power rather than performance. The ultimate measurement must therefore be governance. Does a business licence take days instead of months? Are teachers and doctors present? Are development projects completed on time? Can citizens obtain public services without intermediaries? Can civil servants make lawful professional decisions without seeking political protection? Significantly, the Police Service and Foreign Service would remain outside the proposed NES. There are sound reasons for treating them as specialised career services requiring institutional continuity, accumulated professional experience and service-specific training. Their exclusion from the NES, however, need not mean exclusion from reform. For the police, Pakistan does not need to start from scratch. In May 2018, then chief justice Mian Saqib Nisar initiated a Police Reforms Committee bringing together nine retired and seven serving Inspectors General of Police. After extensive deliberations, it produced the two-volume Police Reforms: Way Forward, launched in Jan 2019. Building upon thePolice Order 2002and subsequent experience, the exercise addressed some of the most persistent weaknesses of policing: accountability, quality and independence of investigation, complaint redressal, urban policing, alternative dispute resolution, counterterrorism and the legal framework governing the police. It proposed a model police law while recognising the constitutional and administrative realities of Pakistan’s federal system. Yet the principal structural problems identified by the committee remain largely unresolved. Its convener, former IGP Afzal Ali Shigri, observed as recently as Feb 2026 that fragmented legal frameworks, weaknesses in investigation and uneven accountability mechanisms continue to impede reform. The 2019 police reform report thus stands as a telling case study of Pakistan’s persistent gap between designing reform and implementing it. The exclusion of the Police Service from the NES presents an opportunity rather than necessarily a deficiency. Instead of forcing policing into an administrative model designed for civilian ministries, the government can revive Police Reforms: Way Forward, update it and implement its still-relevant recommendations. The Foreign Service can similarly retain its distinctive professional structure while pursuing the broader reform principles of merit, specialisation, transparent advancement and measurable performance. The government proposes an ambitious implementation timetable for the new civil-service package. Speed can create momentum, but changing regulations is easier than changing administrative culture. No examination reform can compensate for arbitrary postings. No specialised cadre can flourish if expertise is subordinated to connections. No performance contract creates accountability if influence protects poor performance. And no reform report, however professionally drafted, improves governance while it remains on a shelf. Pakistan has spent decades reforming bureaucracy on paper. The real reform is to build institutions where competence matters more than cadre, performance more than seniority, expertise more than connections and public service more than institutional privilege. The writer is a former Inspector General of Police and DG FIA.
articles.author: Tahsin Shah

articles.title: The politics of free electricity
articles.content: A FEW months ago, I was appointed an independent director on the board of the Sukkur Electric Power Company (Sepco) by the federal minister for power. Having spent nearly two decades working with rural communities in upper Sindh, I saw this as an opportunity to confront a problem widely considered intractable: mass-scale electricity theft in villages. The prevailing wisdom within the power utility is that rural communities cannot be persuaded to pay for electricity. Politicians behave as though electricity is theirs to distribute as political largesse. Voters, in turn, believe they have earned the right to free electricity by supporting those politicians. What should be a straightforward transaction between a utility and its customer is instead an instrument of political patronage. The argument within the company and its political elements is that villagers can’t afford to pay for power. And rural communities consider free electricity a right, simply because that’s the only form of electricity they’ve experienced. My recent experience suggests that the problem is not nearly as insoluble as we have been led to believe. In my own village, where I have worked on integrated development for many years, we initiated an experiment to remove illegal electricity connections, known as kundas, and encourage households to apply for legal meters. Sepco staff removed about 500 illegal connections. The reaction was immediate. Nearly 200 villagers marched in protest to confront me. I invited them in to talk. Electricity theft in Sindh is not exclusively a consumer problem. It is equally a governance problem. During the ensuing community meeting, I asked a simple question. “Have you ever gone to a mobile phone shop and demanded balance for your phone while refusing to pay for it?” “Why not?” I asked. “Because from the first day you used a mobile phone, you knew you had to pay for the service. But from the first day you received electricity, you never paid for it. So you believe that is normal too.” The exchange exposed something fundamental about electricity theft in rural Sindh. It is not simply a matter of poverty or unwillingness to pay. It is a culture of entitlement cultivated over decades, with the active participation of politicians and power company employees. But the villagers’ resistance is not entirely irrational. Many have legitimate fears about becoming legal consumers. Sepco has a history of imposing questionable detection bills. When consumers protest, corrupt officials demand bribes to withdraw or reduce those charges. Why, villagers ask, should they voluntarily enter a system that exposes them to arbitrary billing, harassment and extortion? Some protesters made an especially revealing argument. My term on the Sepco board will end in three years, they pointed out. What happens after that? Who will protect them from detection bills, political interference and corrupt officials? It was a difficult question to answer because their mistrust is rooted in experience. Indeed, one of the greatest obstacles to legalising electricity connections comes from within Sepco itself. During our campaign, company employees actively discouraged villagers from applying for meters, warning them that legal connections would create endless headaches. The reason is not difficult to understand. Illegal connections are a lucrative source of illicit income for employees who facilitate and maintain them. A legal meter threatens not only the culture of free electricity but also the informal economy that has developed around it. This creates a remarkable situation in which the electricity company, supposedly responsible for selling electricity and collecting revenue, has employees with a financial interest in ensuring that neither happens. Simply telling villagers that electricity theft is illegal, or that they have a moral obligation to pay, achieves very little. Those arguments fall on deaf ears when the institution demanding payment has so thoroughly undermined its own credibility. What does work is sustained engagement, backed by practical action and tangible benefits. Before our intervention, villagers typically received just three or four hours of electricity in 24 hours and experienced outages that could last months without repair. Following the removal of illegal connections and improvements to the distribution system, metered households began receiving approximately 16 hours of electricity daily. Any faults were repaired immediately. This was a powerful demonstration of what legalisation could achieve. Instead of an unreliable supply obtained through illegal connections, households could now access substantially more electricity through a legitimate connection. Of approximately 500 illegal connections covered in the initial exercise, around 100 households applied for meters. As those applications came in and the benefits became visible, others began expressing interest. We are now working to extend legal connections to more households and onto more villages. The significance of this experience goes beyond the numbers. It challenges the entrenched assumption that villagers will never pay for electricity. They can. But they need to see a credible alternative to the existing system. That means reliable electricity, transparent billing, protection from arbitrary detection charges and a mechanism for resolving complaints without paying bribes. It also means confronting the employees and political interests that profit from the status quo. Most importantly, it requires treating rural communities as participants in reform rather than merely as offenders to be punished. Electricity theft in Sindh is not exclusively a consumer problem. It is equally a governance problem, sustained by a mutually beneficial arrangement between politicians, corrupt utility employees and consumers accustomed to receiving something for nothing. Breaking that arrangement requires political courage, institutional accountability and patient community engagement. Our experiment has not solved Sepco’s enormous problems. But it has demonstrated something important: the supposedly impossible is possible. This learning could be applied to the whole gamut of problems Sepco finds itself in. The writer is a rural development specialist and social entrepreneur.
articles.author: Naween A. Mangi

articles.title: The AI paradox
articles.content: WE’RE building machines that are smart enough to replace us but not wise enough to save us. That’s the contradiction at the heart of the AI debate, and it’s not hypothetical anymore. In September 2026, Jacob Coxon, an Anthropic researcher, resigned and publicly stated that the people building AI actually believe the technology could end humanity by the end of this decade (Axios, Sept 2026). His colleague Evan Hubinger, Anthropic’s alignment science lead, puts the probability of human extinction in the next 10 years at over 10 per cent. Dario Amodei, who runs Anthropic, went further, warning about a swarm of agents that could take over the internet in six to 12 months if nothing is done (Axios, Sept 2026). The people sounding the alarm are the same ones writing the code. A question that keeps coming back to me is this: what if AI knows everything? What if AI is integrated in every department, in every field? We don’t know the answers, but the reality may be far more dangerous than our worst nightmares. We’re introducing AI into every discipline as though it was designed for it, with no thought for the ramifications. People are using AI to automate their jobs. They’re handing personal details over to AI-powered large language models (CVs, email accounts, all sorts of data associated with a fairly standard job application). It’s quick. It’s efficient. But when the vulnerability exceeds the productivity, we should be limiting that practice or getting rid of it altogether. The people sounding the alarm are the same ones writing the code. What if we don’t actually know what AI is doing with our data? What if it’s hiding information from us and we can’t see that? Its sheer convenience will blind us to the cost. The infrastructure powering AI has a similarly troubling story to tell. As of August 2026, there are some 12,000 active data centres in the world, with over 4,500 of them in the United States alone (Data Centre Map, August 2026). Where will that number be in 10 years? A June 2026 United Nations University report states that in 2025 the world’s data centres consumed 448 trillion watt-hours of electricity, more than all but 10 countries. By 2030, they are expected to account for nearly 3pc of global electricity use, emitting some 400 million metric tonnes of CO2 per year (AP/UN University Report, June 2026). More AI means more data centres. More data centres means more environmental damage. The maths doesn’t lie, and it doesn’t forgive. For Pakistan (ranked the most vulnerable country to climate change in 2022 by the Germanwatch Climate Risk Index), this is no remote threat. The 2022 floods affected a third of the country, killed over 1,700 people and caused damage exceeding $30 billion (Germanwatch CRI 2025). As demand for AI infrastructure grows, so does the pressure on energy systems and the climate, with consequences extending far beyond the countries developing the technology. AI can help with flood forecasting and crop monitoring, yes. But if the technology enabling that is developed without proper governance, then those benefits are meaningless. So, can we just go back to manual systems? In most cases, no. The World Bank’s October 2026 economic update notes that Pakistan is hamstrung by poor broadband penetration, unreliable electricity and a critical lack of digital skills. Nadra’s biometric databases already run using automated systems that would be impractical to replace manually at national scale. Going back to all that is not an option. The real issue isn’t whether we need AI, but how we adopt it responsibly without making the very problems we are trying to survive worse. The issue isn’t AI per se. It’s about planning and execution. If we automate everything, then what do we do by hand? And if that automation becomes uncontrolled, do we even have the option to turn it off? AI development is consuming massive amounts of money and energy, often with no proportional return. Nobody has all the answers. All we can do is demand that any new data centre proposal undergo a mandatory environmental impact assessment before approval. We can demand that AI governance is treated as seriously as AI innovation. If no humans are left, what is the point of AI or its efficiencies? If the world we live in is no longer liveable, no amount of technological development will make any difference. The writer is an AI engineer and researcher.
articles.author: Huzaifa bin Muneer

articles.title: The cost of injustice
articles.content: TO live in Karachi, or really any city in the tumultuous world that is our reality, is an exercise in dodging misfortune. When one leaves the house, one braces for survival. Traffic has to be navigated, angry or errant drivers avoided, beggars ask for money and there is filth on the street. By the time one reaches the destination, one is in a state of high vigilance. Dangers and disruptions are everywhere. This means that most in the city live in a constant state of hypervigilance. Some would say that wealth can insulate a person from this avalanche of potential misfortune. There is material evidence of this: the wealthy have drivers who take them places, their cars and homes are cool with air conditioning and electricity outages are eliminated with generators. They see the best doctors and eat the best food. If you belong to this class, the injustice that you see everywhere in a megacity is made distant. The maimed beggar, the dog being beaten, the woman wrapped in black trying to navigate a street full of men are things that exist in some different world. The car window, the tall gate, the armed guard — these, it is assumed, make the cruelties of the context irrelevant. If they are considered, it is only in a calculation that assures you that your good fortune is deserved and those suffering must have earned it through some arithmetic of divine distribution. The truth is that life in an unjust society exacts a cost. It does not matter how well you may take care of yourself; context matters. In her extraordinary book Weathering: The Extraordinary Stress of Ordinary Life in an Unjust Society, Dr Arline Geronimus has shown that the constant physical toll of coping with injustice can have deep physical and mental consequences. Naturally, the most disadvantaged suffer the worst consequences, but the effects of living amid inequality accrue on everyone in a society. Diseased societies produce diseased people. One category of disadvantaged people in Pakistani society is women. In a world in which patriarchy reigns, women are always playing defence. Marriage is a minefield where, if the demands of a husband or in laws are not met, every day can become a living hell. A long list of dead women that I regularly write about in this column is evidence of this. If a woman is unable to bear a child for instance, she may either face divorce or her husband taking a second wife. If children do come, they can increase a woman’s dependence on her husband, making it harder to resist whatever strictures are imposed upon her. The cost of all this is a constant state of vigilance, and Geronimus showed just how it can physically wear one down. Repeated activation of the stress response can disrupt hormonal regulation, raise blood pressure and contribute to inflammation. In the long term, this increases vulnerability to chronic disease and early death. Diseased societies produce diseased people. A 2021 systematic study and meta-analysis found that 37 per cent of pregnant women experienced antenatal depression, while 30pc experienced postnatal depression. Intimate partner violence and poor relationships with spouses were among the reported risk factors. These figures can be attributed to the fact that women do not feel confident about their own or their children’s futures because they live in a society where injustice is common. The most interesting thing about research on men and women in unjust societies is that men suffer too. Research examining sexism in US states has linked patriarchal contexts to poorer health outcomes in both men and women. People believe that individual actions, status or material wealth can allow them to evade the conditions they see others endure. All this suggests that individual choices and wealth are not the biggest determinants of health in a society. Instead, it is the availability of collective justice and respect for life that affect health outcomes. This should give all Pakistanis pause. The poor are treated horribly, and we see terrible crimes committed against the weak every day. Women are regularly treated like chattel, children are routinely abused and caste and wealth determine the course of one’s life. The worst curse is that we have learned to rationalise all of this, to absorb it as the way things are, the way things have been and the way things will always be. But being inured to injustice and quietly accepting of it is making us sick. Our tolerance of it creeps into our cells and our bones. It is time we understood that there is no individual cure for these conditions and what ails us is a collective issue — deeper and more entrenched than improving our diets, quitting smoking or hitting the gym. Our habit of seeing so many wrongs and ignoring them is quite literally what is killing us. The writer is an attorney teaching constitutional law and political philosophy.
articles.author: Rafia Zakaria

articles.title: China green channel
articles.content: THE agreement between Islamabad and Beijing to set up a green channel at the Sost-Khunjerab border for agricultural and allied products should ease bilateral cross-border trade. Priority customs processing, risk-based inspections and faster clearance of perishables should cut delays and the cost of moving goods. The question is if it will help Pakistan’s agricultural exports. The two customs administrations will share information, including risk alerts, which should speed up inspections without loosening oversight. Quick clearance matters most for farm produce, which spoils if held up, costing growers money and competitiveness. Reliable access to the Chinese market could help farmers and exporters find new buyers and earn more foreign exchange. The trade gap shows how much remains to be done. Last year, Pakistan Customs collected a record Rs15bn in revenue on imports through Khunjerab, while exports to China and Central Asia via the route came to just Rs2.8bn. The two figures measure different things and cannot be compared directly. But they do show how little we export through this corridor. Pakistan needs to identify which agricultural products it can export, meet Chinese quality standards, and build dependable supply chains. Fruit and vegetables from Gilgit-Baltistan and other northern areas stand to gain from better access. However, exporters need cold storage, refrigerated transport, grading and packaging facilities, and predictable logistics. Weather is another constraint. The Khunjerab Pass is generally open for trade and travel from April to November; heavy snow shuts it in winter. Both countries should work towards keeping it open year-round. A green channel is of little use if exporters cannot count on the route for regular deliveries throughout the year. The initiative can also be seen in the wider context of CPEC. Pakistan has tended to treat its economic relationship with Beijing mainly as a source of infrastructure investment and imports. Market access, local business participation and two-way trade deserve equal weight. There is no doubt that exchanging customs documents electronically should remove procedural bottlenecks and also curb under-invoicing of Chinese imports, which remains a serious drain on the exchequer. Beijing’s reported exports exceed Pakistan’s recorded imports from China by around $5bn, a gap that points to large-scale misdeclaration at the border and heavy revenue losses. It is time this too was fixed. Honest valuation would shield local producers and manufacturers from unfair competition and factory closures. The green channel is a useful step, but it should be judged by results: growth in Pakistani exports, the number of businesses reaching the Chinese market, and the income of domestic producers.
articles.author: Editorial

articles.title: Excessive punishment
articles.content: THE supposed ‘crime’ did not justify a trial under terrorism laws, and certainly not the punishment. On Thursday, human rights lawyer Imaan Mazari-Hazir and her husband and fellow lawyer, Hadi Ali Chattha, weresentenced to 10 yearseach for moving a security barrier reportedly placed to protect a touring cricket team, as well as for “incitement to public unrest” during a face-off with police. The trial, held in jail, drew persistent criticism over an alleged lack of due process. The judge held that Ms Mazari-Hazir and Mr Chattha had attempted to “compromise the security arrangements [made for the team] through pressuring security officials”. The judgement cited the 2009 attack on the Sri Lankan cricket team in Lahore — an assault that had been perpetrated by more than a dozen terrorists armed with heavy weapons — to reason that the lawyers’ act of removing the barrier and ‘assaulting’ police personnel “put the security of an international team visiting Pakistan at risk [and] clearly shows the intentions and objective of the accused to create sense of terror [sic]”. Just last month, after a lengthy appeals process, the Supreme Court ordered the suspension of the sentence handed to the two lawyers in the so-calledsocial media posts caseand ordered their release pending the Islamabad High Court’s decision on their appeal against the trial court’s verdict. However, they were promptly rearrested in connection with this case, and have now been handed a lengthy sentence that will keep them behind bars while they appeal. Ms Mazari-Hazir is one of the most prominent champions of civil and human rights from the legal community, and has often taken cases involving some of Pakistan’s most vulnerable citizens pro bono. She is also an outspoken critic of government and state excesses. It is unfortunate to see her and her husband punished so harshly for acts that seem downright frivolous compared to the violence actual terrorists routinely perpetrate. The higher courts must hear their appeal swiftly, and the state must stop stretching antiterrorism laws to cover acts that bear no resemblance to terrorism. Such verdicts send a chilling message to every lawyer willing to defend the vulnerable. The law need only appear to serve narrow interests, rather than justice, for public faith in it to be shaken.
